context: fit-out-led · superflat slab, ESFR fire and material-handling integration drive the programme

brief.intro: A warehouse or distribution centre is essentially a very large, tall steel shed built around two things: a floor flat enough for narrow-aisle forklifts or automated storage/retrieval systems, and a fire-suppression system sized for what will be stored inside it. The building envelope goes up fast — portal-frame steel, metal roof and cladding — so the schedule quickly shifts to the fit-out: the floor slab, racking, conveyors/ASRS and the ESFR sprinkler system that protects the stored goods. Unlike an office building, comfort HVAC is minor; the real drivers are structural-steel lead time, the superflat floor pour, and the fire-engineering approval that fixes what class of sprinkler the racking needs. Material-handling equipment — conveyors, sortation, ASRS — and dock equipment are usually supplied and installed by a specialist subcontractor on a separate track that has to be integrated late in the programme. Because racking height and storage commodity class drive the fire design, a late change to the racking layout is a major schedule risk, not a minor one.

glossary.plain: Early Suppression Fast Response heads — powerful sprinklers that put out a rack fire without needing sprinklers inside the racking itself.
a floor poured dead flat and level so very-narrow-aisle trucks or robots can run safely at speed.
narrow racking aisles serviced by guided forklifts — needs the superflat floor to work safely.
Automated Storage & Retrieval System — robotic cranes or shuttles that store and retrieve pallets without a driver.
a hydraulic ramp that bridges the gap between the warehouse floor and a parked trailer bed.
Warehouse Management System — the software that tells forklifts, conveyors or robots what to move and where.
the steel-frame typology (column plus pitched rafter) most warehouses are built from.
how a fire engineer rates what will be stored — cartons, plastics, aerosols — which sets the sprinkler design.

must_get_right: Fix the racking layout and commodity class before finalising the fire (ESFR) design — a late change reopens the fire engineering and re-drives sprinkler spacing and pump sizing.
Protect the superflat floor pour — it needs a dry, protected slab-on-grade sequence and cannot be revisited once racking is set on it.
Track MHE, conveyors and ASRS as a separate specialist scope with its own long lead time, feeding into commissioning rather than assumed as part of the base build.
Sequence dock equipment and yard pavement to be ready with structural completion — trucks need the yard before goods-in testing can start.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and structural steel run a 6-day week to protect the weathertight date; the superflat slab pour runs on a continuous-pour calendar once started and cannot be interrupted mid-bay; racking and MHE installation follows the specialist subcontractor's own calendar, typically two shifts near go-live.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs structural steel fabrication & erection → weathertight envelope → superflat floor slab → racking layout freeze & fire-engineering sign-off → ESFR installation → MHE/ASRS installation → WMS integration → commissioning. Structural steel is rarely critical once fabricated — it erects quickly — but the floor slab and the fire-engineering freeze that gates ESFR installation usually are.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen and the racking layout finalised before the fire-engineering submission; a single mobilisation; the client's MHE/WMS supplier integrates against an agreed interface schedule; no free-issue equipment assumed unless stated.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is fit-out-led once the shell is up. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: ESFR sprinkler heads & fire pump package

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Crane and laydown access for steel erection; the floor-slab pour needs a large continuous-pour crew and a weather-protected, dust-free sequence; racking and MHE installation need a clean, secure, access-controlled area; commissioning of ASRS needs power and controls ready ahead of the mechanical trades.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: a late racking-layout change reopening the fire-engineering design, structural-steel delivery delay, floor-flatness rework, and MHE/ASRS commissioning re-test loops. Schedule contingency is held before MHE go-live and before WMS integration rather than spread across the fit-out.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
